Part 4 You will hear a zoology lecturer talking about
a group of primitive animals called gastropods. First you have some time to look at questions
31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
Good morning everyone. In this module we've been looking at various field survey methods
and now I'm going to give you a brief introduction to the specific organism that will be
focusing on during our first field trip, and that's the gastropod. Gastropods are invertebrates,
their organisms without a backbone, and they're more commonly known as snails or, if they
haven't got a shell, slugs. Now, in terms of their evolution, gastropods go back a
long way. As with other primitive animals, the minerals in their body fluids are very
similar to the mineral composition of the sea, indicating that they began life there. And
their fossilised remains have been found in rocks dating back at least 500 million years.
Looking at the physical features of the gastropods, well, they all have one muscular foot for
swimming or walking. This foot is lubricated with mucus, and it's this that leaves the
sticky trail that you see behind snails and slugs. They also have an organ called a
radula, which they use for feeding. Then of course the snails, though not the
slugs, have a shell. In terms of their dimensions, snail shells in Britain range
from the dwarf snail, which is 1.5 millimeters long, to the Roman snail,
whose shell can be as big as 50 millimeters. As well as size variations,
variations, you get a lot of differences in the form of snail shells. For example, the
majority coil to the right, but there are a few that coil to the left. Then some shells,
for instance, the plated snail, have regularly spaced ribs, while the prickly snail has
prominent spines. There are even a number of species with hair on their shells. Colours
on the shells also vary as do patterns, so appearances are really varied.
Okay, let's turn now to feeding habits. Most of you who are gardeners will know to
your cost that some gastropods eat healthy plants. But you may not realise that these
are the minority. Most species feed on rotting plants, or they eat fungi and algae. Some
are some that are actually carnivorous. They prey on live animals. For example, the shield
slug feuds on worms. And apart from their own feeding habits, I should point out that
gastropods themselves have plenty of predators. Birds and frogs are the main ones. But there's
even an entire family of flies that have specialised in preying on gastropods.
And of course, last but not least, I should mention human predators.
It was the Romans who probably first introduced edible snails into Britain during the first
century and they are still eaten today.
In fact, the collection of wild snails for cooking has caused local extinctions of
one species, which is also under threat internationally.
So, there are lots of predators, but to protect themselves, gastropods have often developed
special defences.
I'll just give you one example.
The glutinous snail avoids predators by folding its mantle over its shell and turning itself
into a very slippery blob of jelly.
Well, turning now to gastropod habitats, most species like dampness and shade.
In general, both very hot and very cold weather is bad for gastropods, but dry conditions
are the least favourable. Snails cope with this by withdrawing into their shells, and
often they form a thick film of mucus over the mouth of their shell to minimise loss
of water. Habitats with a long, stable history tend to support the biggest range of gastropod
species. So, for instance, long-established forests usually support more species than
newer plantations of trees, and old, natural meadowland is much better than land which
has recently been farmed. And there is a small number of highly-specialised species that
live in unusual habitats. For instance, the blind snail spends its whole life buried
under the ground. It's been reported living at depths of two metres, and particularly
likes the cavities in old, buried bones apparently. But species like these are exceptional.
But wherever they live, gastropods are often sensitive to pollution, and they don't thrive
in areas contaminated by agrochemicals. This means that they are a reliable indication
of how healthy our environment is.
Now, at this point, I'd like to consider Habitat and Management.

1.why: "It's a studio, so basically it's designed for a single person or a couple".

2.why: "Every two apartments in the building share a separate laundry".

3.why: "You look right out over the harbour. It's a pretty awesome view".

4.why: Khách muốn có vườn nhưng toà nhà không có; "your apartment has a balcony, so there's room to sit out there".

5.why: Có phòng gym ở tầng 1, "all residents have access to that free of charge".

6.why: "It even has a couple of cinemas" (a couple = two); mở cho công chúng nhưng cư dân được giảm giá.

7.why: Khách hỏi "Is that underground?" – "That's right". Chỗ trống điền parking.

8.why: Khách đặt mức tối đa $600; giá thực tế "this comes in at $580". Bẫy: 600 là ngân sách, không phải tiền thuê.

9.why: Nhiều nơi phải trả thêm "the cost of electricity, but in this case it's all included".

10.why: Người thuê cũ đi ngày 8, dọn dẹp ngày 10 hoặc 11, "it'll be free from the 13th".

11.why: Có 20 lối vào, "each connected to public roads by short paths" → B. Bẫy: xe buýt chỉ tới 2 điểm đầu cuối (C), bãi đỗ có camera chỉ ở 4 lối vào (A).

12.why: "In response to a poll of walkers last year, we've recently installed kiosks… with clear, easy-to-follow maps and other trail information" → C. Picnic và chỗ sạc đã có từ trước.

13.why: Red Rock Walk là cơ hội "to study a huge variety of vegetation" → A. Không nhìn được xa (B sai), chim thì "hard to spot" (C sai).

14.why: Mùa đông "if the weather conditions are really unsuitable, we might have to close this walk" → C. Sông vẫn đóng băng, tuyết dày (B sai) và thường đông người (A sai).

15.why: Giường tập thể: đặt trước không hiệu quả "so now we allocate them as people arrive" → H (ai đến trước được trước).

16.why: Phòng gia đình: "you will need to make arrangements ahead of time" → F (phải đặt trước).

17.why: "A popular facility that we've recently added is coin-operated washing machines" → G (thiết bị mới).

18.why: Bữa ăn có giá cố định, nhưng "We do ask you to give a hand with serving and cleaning up after meals" → D (nhờ khách giúp). Bẫy I: giá như nhau cho người lớn và trẻ em.

19.why: Tắm nước nóng "at no charge" → E (miễn phí).

20.why: "The hostel is in the process of creating a bike rental scheme which should be up and running next year" → C (chưa có).

21.why: Thuyết thiếu vitamin D dựa vào việc người Anh bỏ dầu gan cá, "but it was only in Britain that cod liver oil was so popular, so that argument doesn't really make sense" → C.

22.why: "When plants are exposed to more CO2 they produce more pollen" → C. Bẫy B: CO2 ảnh hưởng "as much as milder winters", không phải ít hơn.

23.why: Dự báo dài hạn mùa xuân đến sớm hơn, "but that doesn't mean that spring will come earlier every year" – năm ngoái muộn, năm nay sớm → không có xu hướng rõ trong ngắn hạn (A).

24.why: Ragweed là ví dụ cây "moving into new areas", nay bắt đầu mọc ở châu Âu "for the first time" → A. Nó là tác nhân chính ở Mỹ, không phải ở mọi nơi (B sai).

25.why: Ở thành phố "so many hard surfaces… the pollen doesn't get absorbed so much" → B. Việc cấm trồng một số cây là hệ quả, không phải lý do (C sai).

26.why: Áo: "here we've only got data for birch pollen" → G.

27.why: Pháp: mùa phấn bắt đầu sớm hơn với sồi và bạch dương, "but it doesn't start any earlier for grass" → B (thay đổi ở hai loại).

28.why: Hà Lan: "oak pollen is starting much earlier. Eighteen days" – nước khác không chênh lớn vậy → A.

29.why: Thuỵ Sĩ: mùa phấn bắt đầu sớm hơn "for oak, birch and grass" → D (tất cả các loại).

30.why: Anh: "wet summers have extended the grass pollen season from 5 weeks to 8 weeks" → C.

31.why: Khoáng chất trong dịch cơ thể "very similar to the mineral composition of the sea".

32.why: "The majority coil to the right, but there are a few that coil to the left".

33.why: Có gờ (ribs), gai (spines), và "a number of species with hair on their shells".

35.why: Người La Mã "first introduced edible snails into Britain during the first century".

36.why: "Gastropods have often developed special defences" – ví dụ ốc glutinous biến thành khối thạch trơn.

37.why: Nóng hay lạnh đều hại, "but dry conditions are the least favourable" (least favourable = worst).

38.why: "Long-established forests usually support more species than newer plantations".

39.why: "The blind snail spends its whole life buried under the ground".

40.why: Chúng nhạy với ô nhiễm nên "a reliable indication of how healthy our environment is".
